steps.body:
Counting outcomes and finding probabilities are the same move, divided by the total. If every card is equally likely, P(A) is just |A|/52. So the overlap correction you learned for **counts** carries straight over to **probabilities**:

P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B).
The deck laid out as a 4 × 13 grid — one cell per card.

widget.prompt: Shade P(heart **or** face card). The 3 face-card hearts get shaded once, not twice.
widget.successFeedback: 22 of 52 cells: 10 plain hearts + 3 face-card hearts + 9 face cards in other suits. That is 13 + 12 − 3.
widget.lowFeedback: Smaller than the whole shaded region. Every heart counts, and so does every J, Q or K in any suit.
widget.highFeedback: Larger than 22 cells — a common cause is shading the 3 face-card hearts twice, once for each event.

predict.prompt: You'll shade 11/26 of the grid. Will that cover more or less than half of it?
predict.reveal: Half means the numerator is half the denominator — 13/26 here — and 11 is less. Against a big denominator like 26, 11 cells look substantial — which is exactly why "more than half" tempts — but halving the denominator settles any near case like this one. Probability as shaded area makes the benchmark visible before you count a single cell.

cml.actionGoal: Select regions of an equal-outcome sample space and coordinate area with event probability.

steps.body: Name the rule, not just the number.
explanationVariants: P(heart) = 13/52 and P(face) = 12/52, but the 3 face-card hearts sit in both, so subtract 3/52 once: 22/52.
Count the grid: 22 shaded cells out of 52. The straight sum 13 + 12 = 25 is 3 too many — exactly the size of the overlap.

widget.prompt: Which expression gives P(heart or face card)?

options.feedback: That is the addition rule: add both events, then remove the double-counted overlap once.
That sum counts the 3 face-card hearts in both terms, so it reports 25 cards where the grid shows only 22.
The overlap gets added twice, so it must come off exactly once. Subtracting it twice erases those 3 cards from the union entirely.
Multiplying answers a different question — "heart AND face" — and even then this product is not how you would find it.

explanationVariants: Multiples of 3: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18 → 6. Multiples of 5: 5, 10, 15, 20 → 4. Ticket 15 is on both lists, so 6 + 4 − 1 = 9.
List the winners in order: 3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 12, 15, 18, 20. Nine distinct tickets — 15 appears once, because a ticket is one ticket.

widget.prompt: Tickets 1–20. You win if your number is a multiple of 3 **or** a multiple of 5. How many of the 20 tickets win?

commonErrors.feedback: That is 6 + 4. Ticket 15 is a multiple of both, so a plain sum counts it twice — subtract it once.
That is the multiples of 3 alone. The multiples of 5 win too: 5, 10, 20 add three more (15 is already counted).
That is the overlap — ticket 15 only. The overlap is what you subtract, not the answer.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Six multiples of 3, four multiples of 5, and 15 is on both lists: 6 + 4 − 1 = 9.

steps.body:
When the overlap is empty, P(A ∩ B) = 0 and the subtraction does nothing:

P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B).

That is the *special* case, not the default. Adding without checking the overlap is the single most common error in this chapter — so before you add, always ask: **can both happen at once?**
One roll of a fair die.
explanationVariants: Sort by whether a single roll can satisfy both events. "Even" and "shows 5" cannot — 5 is odd. "Even" and "more than 4" both hold for 6, so they overlap.
Write the sets. Even = {2, 4, 6}. The set {5} misses all of them, so no overlap. The set {5, 6} shares the 6. Primes on a die are {2, 3, 5}, and 2 is even — so primes overlap the evens too.

widget.prompt: Roll one die. For each pair of events, can they both happen on the SAME roll?

items.label: even · shows a 5
items.feedback: 5 is odd, so no roll is both. The events are mutually exclusive and the probabilities add straight: 3/6 + 1/6.

items.label: even · greater than 4
items.feedback: A 6 is even AND greater than 4, so the events share an outcome. Subtract that one.

items.label: less than 3 · greater than 3
items.feedback: A single roll lands below 3 or above 3, never both, so these events share no outcome. Add straight.

items.label: even · prime
items.feedback: 2 is even and prime, so the events share the outcome 2.

widget.missFeedback: For each pair, hunt for a single face that satisfies both. If one exists, the events overlap.
widget.successFeedback: Sorted. Only the pairs that share a face — even/greater-than-4 (the 6) and even/prime (the 2) — need the subtraction.

explanationVariants: Even = {2, 4, 6}; greater than 4 = {5, 6}. The 6 is in both, so 3 + 2 − 1 = 4 faces: 2, 4, 5, 6.
Just list the union: 2, 4, 5, 6. Four faces out of six — the 6 belongs to the union once, however many events it satisfies.

widget.prompt: Roll one die. How many faces are **even or greater than 4**?

commonErrors.feedback: That is 3 + 2. The face 6 is even AND greater than 4, so it was counted twice — remove it once.
That is "greater than 4" alone ({5, 6}). The evens 2 and 4 also belong to the union.
That is the overlap ({6}), the quantity you subtract — not the size of the union.

steps.body: One card, one rule, three ways to go wrong.
hints: Two events: RED and ACE. Get each count first, then ask what sits in both.
There are 26 red cards and 4 aces — but the ace of hearts and the ace of diamonds are on both lists.
So the union is 26 + 4 − 2 = 28 cards. Now divide by 52 and round to three decimals.
explanationVariants: Count the black aces instead: only 2 aces are new information, since the red ones are already inside the 26 red cards. 26 + 2 = 28 → 28/52 ≈ 0.538.

widget.prompt: Draw one card from 52. Find **P(red or ace)** as a decimal, rounded to three places.

commonErrors.feedback: That is 30/52 — the straight sum 26 + 4. The two red aces belong to both events, so they were counted twice.
That is P(red) alone, 26/52. The two black aces are also in the union and were never counted.
That is 2/52, the overlap of red and ace. The overlap is subtracted inside the rule; it is not the answer.

takeaways: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B) — add, then take the overlap back once.
Mutually exclusive events are the special case where the overlap is 0 and plain addition is safe.
Before adding any two probabilities, ask: can both happen at the same time?
steps.teaser: Next: a table that shows every joint and marginal probability at once.

concept.body: Adding P(A) and P(B) counts everything in the middle **twice** — once from each event. The rule fixes that by subtracting the middle once. If the events cannot co-occur, the middle is empty and there is nothing to subtract.

explanationVariants: 8 + 6 = 14 counts the 2 both-players twice, so the union is 14 − 2 = 12.
Only-soccer is 8 − 2 = 6 and only-tennis is 6 − 2 = 4, so 6 + 4 + 2 = 12 play at least one.

widget.prompt: In a club, 8 play soccer, 6 play tennis, and 2 play both. How many play **at least one**?

commonErrors.feedback: That is 8 + 6 with no correction — the 2 who play both appear in each total, so they are counted twice.
That subtracts the 2 twice. They do play, so they belong in the union exactly once: 8 + 6 − 2.
